title: The Biometric Mandate and the Nine-Judge Charter of Fundamental Privacy
hook: A unanimous nine-judge Constitution Bench declared privacy an intrinsic fundamental right protected against arbitrary state intrusion.
laws: Constitution of India (Article 14, Article 19, and Article 21)

facts.label: Court
facts.value: Supreme Court of India (Nine-Judge Constitution Bench)

facts.label: Origin of Dispute
facts.value: Constitutional challenge to a nationwide biometric identification program launched without initial statutory backing

facts.label: Precedents Reconsidered
facts.value: Two earlier larger-bench rulings from 1954 and 1962 that had doubted constitutional privacy protection

facts.label: Bench Consensus
facts.value: Unanimous nine-to-zero verdict affirming privacy across six concurring opinions

summary: When the Union government rolled out a massive biometric identification program collecting fingerprints and iris scans from hundreds of millions of residents without an enabling parliamentary statute, a retired High Court judge petitioned the Supreme Court. The petitioner contended that compelling citizens to surrender intimate biological markers to a centralized database under threat of exclusion from essential welfare benefits violated personal liberty and bodily autonomy.

In response, the Union government argued before the court that the Constitution contained no explicit fundamental right to privacy, relying on two earlier larger-bench decisions from 1954 and 1962. Because smaller benches in later decades had recognized privacy in isolated contexts such as wiretapping and medical confidentiality, a three-judge bench referred the foundational constitutional question to an extraordinary nine-judge Constitution Bench.

On August 24, 2017, all nine judges unanimously held that the right to privacy is an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and the freedoms guaranteed across Part III of the Constitution. Overruling the discordant observations in the 1954 and 1962 precedents as well as a notorious 1976 emergency-era ruling, the bench established a strict three-part test of legality, legitimate state aim, and proportionality for any state intrusion into personal, informational, or decisional privacy.

judgment.outcome: Reference answered unanimously (9:0); the right to privacy is declared an intrinsic fundamental right under Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution, overruling prior contrary larger-bench observations.
points: Privacy is a natural, inalienable right inherent in human dignity and liberty rather than a privilege conferred by the State.
The fundamental right to privacy encompasses bodily integrity, informational privacy, and personal autonomy over intimate choices.
Earlier decisions from 1954 and 1962 denying a constitutional right to privacy were rooted in an obsolete siloed reading of fundamental rights and stand overruled.
Any state action or law infringing privacy must satisfy a threefold test: existence of a valid law, a legitimate state aim, and proportionality between means and ends.

principles.name: Proportionality Standard for Rights Restrictions
principles.meaning: Any state measure that limits a fundamental right must be backed by enacted law, pursue a legitimate objective, be suitable and necessary, and avoid disproportionate harm.
principles.inThisCase: The court mandated that future laws collecting or processing citizen data must satisfy strict proportionality and procedural safeguards against abuse.

principles.name: Interrelationship of Fundamental Rights
principles.meaning: Constitutional guarantees of equality, free expression, and personal liberty are not isolated silos; they overlap and reinforce one another.
principles.inThisCase: The bench rejected the siloed approach of early constitutional cases, locating privacy across Articles 14, 19, and 21.

principles.name: Informational Self-Determination
principles.meaning: Individuals retain the right to control how their personal, biometric, and digital data are collected, stored, and disseminated by state or private actors.
principles.inThisCase: The court recognized that in a digital society, unauthorized profiling and unchecked surveillance threaten individual autonomy and democratic dissent.

takeaways: Privacy is a constitutionally protected fundamental right covering the human body, personal information, and intimate life choices.
The State cannot collect biometric or personal data without clear statutory authority, a legitimate public purpose, and proportional safeguards.
This unanimous charter laid the constitutional foundation for later rulings protecting personal autonomy, digital data, and decisional freedom.

lawNote: This constitutional reference interpreted fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21 of the Constitution of India, which remain unchanged and govern both physical and digital state actions.

social.hook: Did you know the government once argued in court that citizens have no fundamental right to privacy?
social.script: Did you know the government once argued in court that citizens have no fundamental right to privacy? When a mandatory biometric database began collecting fingerprints and iris scans from hundreds of millions of residents without a law, a ninety-one-year-old retired judge challenged the state in the Supreme Court. State lawyers claimed the Constitution never guaranteed privacy over one's own body. Nine judges assembled and unanimously rejected that claim, declaring privacy an inalienable fundamental right under Article 21 and establishing strict proportionality limits on state power. You be the judge. Full case notes are on the Courtroom Chronicles website.
social.caption: When the State claimed citizens lacked a constitutional right to privacy over their own bodies, a ninety-one-year-old retired judge led a historic battle that transformed digital and personal liberty forever.
